categories.name: Install and maintain network security controls
categories.blurb: Put barriers like firewalls between your card systems and the rest of the world, and keep them tuned over time.

categories.name: Apply secure configurations to all system components
categories.blurb: Harden every device and system before it goes live instead of trusting the settings it shipped with.

categories.name: Protect stored account data
categories.blurb: Only keep the card data you truly need, and lock down whatever you do store.

categories.name: Protect cardholder data with strong cryptography during transmission
categories.blurb: Scramble card details whenever they travel across networks you do not fully control.

categories.name: Protect all systems and networks from malicious software
categories.blurb: Guard your systems against viruses and other malware and keep those defenses current.

categories.name: Develop and maintain secure systems and software
categories.blurb: Build software safely, patch known holes quickly, and manage changes carefully.

categories.name: Restrict access to system components and cardholder data by business need to know
categories.blurb: Give people access to card data only when their job actually requires it.

categories.name: Identify users and authenticate access to system components
categories.blurb: Make sure every person has a unique login and prove who they are before granting access.

categories.name: Restrict physical access to cardholder data
categories.blurb: Keep the physical places and devices that touch card data away from unauthorized hands.

categories.name: Log and monitor all access to system components and cardholder data
categories.blurb: Record who does what with card systems and review those records to catch problems.

categories.name: Test security of systems and networks regularly
categories.blurb: Routinely probe your own defenses so you find weaknesses before attackers do.

categories.name: Support information security with organizational policies and programs
categories.blurb: Back up your technical controls with clear policies, training, and accountability.

questions.text: Do you have firewalls or equivalent network controls placed between your card-handling systems and untrusted networks like the internet?
questions.why: Without a barrier at the edge, attackers on the open internet can reach systems that handle card data directly.
questions.fix: Deploy a firewall or network security control at every boundary between your card environment and outside networks.

questions.text: Have you written down the rules your firewalls enforce and confirmed each allowed connection has a real business reason?
questions.why: Undocumented or unjustified openings quietly widen the attack surface and often outlive the need that created them.
questions.fix: Document every permitted network path and its business justification, then remove any rule that no longer applies.

questions.text: Is inbound and outbound traffic to your card environment limited to only what is necessary and blocked by default?
questions.why: A permissive default lets unexpected connections slip through and gives malware an easy path in or out.
questions.fix: Set your controls to deny all traffic by default and explicitly allow only the connections you have justified.

questions.text: Do you review your network security rules at least periodically to confirm they are still correct and needed?
questions.why: Network rules drift over time as systems change, leaving stale openings that no one is watching.
questions.fix: Schedule a recurring review of firewall and router configurations and prune anything outdated.

questions.text: Do you change default passwords and other vendor-supplied default settings before putting a system into use?
questions.why: Default credentials are public knowledge and are among the first things attackers try.
questions.fix: Replace every default password and account and adjust risky default settings before deployment.

questions.text: Have you created hardening standards that spell out secure settings for each type of system you run?
questions.why: Without an agreed baseline, systems get configured inconsistently and weak spots go unnoticed.
questions.fix: Adopt configuration standards based on recognized hardening guidance and apply them to every new build.

questions.text: Do you turn off or remove services, ports, and features on your systems that you do not actually need?
questions.why: Every extra service running is one more thing that can be exploited or misconfigured.
questions.fix: Inventory what each system runs and disable anything not required for its job.

questions.text: Is administrative access to your systems always carried over encrypted connections rather than in plain text?
questions.why: Managing systems over unencrypted channels lets anyone watching the network capture admin credentials.
questions.fix: Require encrypted protocols such as SSH or TLS for all remote administration and disable clear-text alternatives.

questions.text: Do you avoid storing card data you do not need, and delete stored card data once its business purpose is over?
questions.why: Data you never keep cannot be stolen, so needless retention only grows your risk.
questions.fix: Set retention limits, and securely purge stored card data when it is no longer required.

questions.text: Are you certain you never keep sensitive authentication data like the full stripe, card verification code, or PIN after authorization?
questions.why: This especially sensitive data lets a thief clone cards or complete fraudulent purchases, so it must never be retained.
questions.fix: Confirm no system or log keeps these elements after authorization and remove any that does.

questions.text: Do you mask card numbers when displayed so only the parts people genuinely need to see are shown?
questions.why: Showing full card numbers on screens or receipts exposes them to shoulder surfing and casual theft.
questions.fix: Mask card numbers by default and reveal the full value only to the few roles with a documented need.

questions.text: Is any card number you store rendered unreadable, for example through strong encryption, truncation, or tokenization?
questions.why: If stored card numbers sit in readable form, a single breach hands attackers usable data.
questions.fix: Protect stored card numbers with strong encryption, truncation, or tokens, and safeguard the keys separately.

questions.text: Do you encrypt card data with strong cryptography whenever it travels across open or public networks like the internet?
questions.why: Card data sent in the clear can be intercepted anywhere along its path across public networks.
questions.fix: Enforce strong transport encryption such as current TLS for every transmission of card data over open networks.

questions.text: Do you rely only on trusted keys and certificates and reject weak or outdated encryption protocols and ciphers?
questions.why: Obsolete protocols and untrusted certificates can be broken or spoofed, defeating the point of encryption.
questions.fix: Disable legacy protocols and weak ciphers, and accept connections only with trusted, valid certificates.

questions.text: Do you make sure card numbers are never sent through end-user messaging tools such as email, chat, or text without protection?
questions.why: Everyday messaging channels are rarely encrypted and leave copies of card data scattered in inboxes and logs.
questions.fix: Prohibit unprotected card data in messaging tools and offer a secure channel when transmission is unavoidable.

questions.text: Do you run anti-malware protection on the systems that are commonly targeted by viruses and other malicious software?
questions.why: Unprotected systems can be silently infected and turned into a foothold for stealing card data.
questions.fix: Install reputable anti-malware software on all susceptible systems and confirm it is actively running.

questions.text: Is your anti-malware kept up to date and set to scan automatically rather than relying on manual checks?
questions.why: Outdated or dormant protection misses new threats and gives infections room to spread.
questions.fix: Enable automatic updates and scheduled scans so protection stays current without manual effort.

questions.text: Are your anti-malware defenses configured so that regular users cannot disable or tamper with them?
questions.why: Protection that a user or attacker can switch off provides no real defense when it matters most.
questions.fix: Lock anti-malware settings so only authorized administrators can change or turn them off.

questions.text: Do you keep track of security vulnerabilities and apply vendor patches promptly, prioritizing the most serious ones?
questions.why: Unpatched known flaws are one of the most common ways attackers break into systems.
questions.fix: Track new vulnerabilities from reliable sources and install critical patches within a defined short window.

questions.text: Do your developers follow secure coding practices that guard against common flaws when you build your own software?
questions.why: Insecure code introduces weaknesses like injection or broken access control that attackers readily exploit.
questions.fix: Train developers in secure coding and review code for common vulnerability classes before release.

questions.text: Do you review and approve changes to your systems and applications before they go into production?
questions.why: Unmanaged changes can silently introduce security holes or break existing protections.
questions.fix: Adopt a change-control process that requires testing and approval before changes reach live systems.

questions.text: Do you protect your public-facing web applications against attacks, for example with regular testing or a web application firewall?
questions.why: Internet-facing applications are constantly probed and are a frequent entry point for card data theft.
questions.fix: Assess web apps for vulnerabilities regularly or place an automated protection layer in front of them.

questions.text: Do you grant access to card data and related systems based on what each person's role actually requires?
questions.why: Broad access means a single compromised account can reach far more data than it should.
questions.fix: Define access by job role and give each person only the minimum needed to do their work.

questions.text: Are your systems set to deny access by default so people get in only where access has been explicitly granted?
questions.why: A default that allows access lets people reach data no one ever deliberately approved.
questions.fix: Configure access controls to deny everything by default and allow only what has been assigned.

questions.text: Do you review who has access to card data periodically and remove permissions that are no longer justified?
questions.why: Access tends to accumulate as people change roles, leaving old permissions that expand risk.
questions.fix: Run periodic access reviews and revoke any rights that no longer match a person's current job.

questions.text: Does every person have their own unique account rather than sharing logins with others?
questions.why: Shared accounts make it impossible to tell who did what, undermining accountability and investigations.
questions.fix: Issue a unique ID to each user and eliminate shared or generic login accounts.

questions.text: Do you enforce strong passwords or passphrases along with sensible rules for how they are set and changed?
questions.why: Weak or reused passwords are easily guessed or cracked, opening the door to your systems.
questions.fix: Require sufficiently long, complex credentials and enforce them through your system settings.

questions.text: Do you require multi-factor authentication for access into the card environment and for all remote and administrative access?
questions.why: A stolen password alone should not be enough to get in, and a second factor stops most account takeovers.
questions.fix: Turn on multi-factor authentication for card-environment, remote, and admin access.

questions.text: Do you promptly disable or remove accounts for people who leave or no longer need access?
questions.why: Lingering accounts for former staff are a favorite target because no one is monitoring them.
questions.fix: Tie account removal to your offboarding process so access is revoked as soon as it ends.

questions.text: Do you control physical entry to areas where card data or the systems handling it are located?
questions.why: Someone who can physically reach a server or storage can bypass many digital protections.
questions.fix: Restrict entry to sensitive areas with locks, badges, or other controls and log who enters.

questions.text: Do you tell visitors apart from staff and escort or monitor them while they are in sensitive areas?
questions.why: An unescorted visitor could tamper with equipment or walk off with media containing card data.
questions.fix: Issue visitor identification, escort guests in sensitive areas, and keep a record of their visits.

questions.text: Do you securely store and, when no longer needed, destroy any physical media or paper that holds card data?
questions.why: Discarded receipts, printouts, or drives can be recovered from the trash by anyone looking.
questions.fix: Lock up media containing card data and shred or wipe it beyond recovery before disposal.

questions.text: Do you inspect card-reading devices like payment terminals for signs of tampering or unauthorized substitution?
questions.why: Criminals tamper with or swap payment terminals to skim card data as customers pay.
questions.fix: Keep an inventory of payment devices and check them regularly for tampering or swaps.

questions.text: Do you record audit logs that capture user activity and access to card data across your systems?
questions.why: Without logs you cannot tell what happened during an incident or spot misuse as it occurs.
questions.fix: Enable logging on all card-handling systems to capture who accessed what and when.

questions.text: Do you review your logs regularly, ideally with automated tools, to catch suspicious or unusual activity?
questions.why: Logs that no one looks at let attacks continue undetected until real damage is done.
questions.fix: Set up routine log review, using automated alerting to surface anomalies quickly.

questions.text: Are your logs protected from tampering and retained long enough to support an investigation?
questions.why: Attackers often try to erase logs, and short retention can wipe out evidence before a breach is noticed.
questions.fix: Store logs securely with tamper protection and keep them for an adequate retention period.

questions.text: Do you keep accurate time across your systems using a trusted time source so log timestamps line up?
questions.why: If clocks disagree, reconstructing the sequence of events during an investigation becomes unreliable.
questions.fix: Synchronize all systems to a trusted time source and protect that time configuration.

questions.text: Do you scan your systems for vulnerabilities on a regular schedule and after significant changes?
questions.why: New weaknesses appear constantly, and regular scanning is how you find them before attackers do.
questions.fix: Run internal and external vulnerability scans periodically and remediate what they uncover.

questions.text: Do you carry out penetration testing periodically to see whether your defenses can actually be breached?
questions.why: Scans find known flaws, but hands-on testing reveals how they could be chained into a real breach.
questions.fix: Commission penetration tests of your card environment and fix the weaknesses they demonstrate.

questions.text: Do you use intrusion detection and tools that alert you to unauthorized changes on critical systems?
questions.why: Early warning of intrusions or unexpected file changes lets you respond before attackers dig in.
questions.fix: Deploy intrusion detection and change-monitoring tools that alert staff to suspicious activity.

questions.text: Do you watch payment pages for unauthorized changes to scripts and page content that could skim card data?
questions.why: Attackers inject malicious scripts into checkout pages to quietly harvest card details from customers.
questions.fix: Monitor and control the scripts running on payment pages and alert on unexpected changes.

questions.text: Do you have a written information security policy that is kept current and shared with everyone it applies to?
questions.why: Without a documented policy, security expectations are inconsistent and hard to enforce.
questions.fix: Publish an information security policy, review it at least yearly, and communicate it to your people.

questions.text: Do you assess your risks and provide security awareness training so staff understand their responsibilities?
questions.why: People who do not understand the risks are more likely to make the mistakes attackers count on.
questions.fix: Run regular risk assessments and give staff ongoing security awareness training.

questions.text: Do you have an incident response plan that spells out how you will detect, react to, and recover from a breach?
questions.why: When a breach hits, a rehearsed plan is the difference between a contained event and a runaway crisis.
questions.fix: Document an incident response plan, assign roles, and test it so the team knows what to do.

questions.text: Do you manage the security risk of third parties who handle card data on your behalf and confirm their compliance?
questions.why: A vendor's weak security can expose your customers' card data just as surely as your own gaps.
questions.fix: Keep a list of service providers, define security responsibilities in contracts, and verify their compliance.
